tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.text:
## Digest email pipeline

The digest is a once-an-hour sweep. An in-process scheduler (or an external cron hitting an HTTP route) calls `runDigestEmailJob`. That job picks orgs whose configured UTC hour matches, then for each subscribed member it collects that member's unread notifications from the trailing 24 hours and "sends" them. In this codebase, sending only writes a log line. I read the code but did not run the test suite.

### 1. What triggers it

Both entry points call `runDigestEmailJob(now)` in `src/server/jobs/digest-email-job.ts`.

**Primary: the in-process scheduler.**
1. `src/instrumentation.ts` `register()` runs once per server process, Node runtime only. It calls `registerEventHandlers()` (`src/server/services/event-registry.ts`) and `startScheduler()`.
2. `startScheduler()` in `src/server/jobs/scheduler.ts` starts a 60-second `setInterval`, unref'd, that calls `tick(new Date())`.
3. `tick()` walks `CADENCE_MINUTES`, where `"digest-email"` is 60. `isDue()` compares against an in-memory `lastRunAt` map. If the kind is due, `tick()` enqueues a job with id `digest-email:<minute>` and calls `drain()`.
4. `drain()` in `src/server/jobs/queue.ts` takes up to 25 due jobs. `runHandler()` dynamically imports the digest module and calls `runDigestEmailJob(new Date())`. A thrown error is retried with exponential backoff, up to 5 attempts.

In practice this means one run per hour, at whatever minute the process started.

**Secondary: `POST /api/cron/digest`** (`src/app/api/cron/digest/route.ts`).
- `assertCronSecret()` in `src/app/api/_lib/responses.ts` requires the header `x-taskflow-cron` to equal `TASKFLOW_CRON_SECRET`. If the secret is unset, it refuses.
- The route calls `runDigestEmailJob(new Date())` directly, bypassing the queue and cadence. The repo contains no cron configuration, so something external must call it.

**Dead path: `digest.due`.** `registerDigestBridge()` in `event-registry.ts` would turn a `digest.due` event into a queued job. Nothing in `src` emits that event, and `runHandler` ignores the payload anyway.

### 2. Which organizations are due

Inside `runDigestEmailJob`, in order:
1. `usageRepo.listOrgIdsForRollup(50)` (`src/server/repositories/usage-repository.ts`) returns the 50 `organization_usage` rows with the oldest `measuredAt`. This is the only org source. An org with no usage row is never considered.
2. `orgRepo.findOrgById()` loads each org.
3. `shouldRunForOrg(org, now)`, exported from the same file, returns false if `archivedAt` is set. Otherwise it requires `now.getUTCHours() === org.settings.digestHourUtc`. Minutes are ignored. The default hour is 7, set in `src/server/db/schema/organizations.ts`.
4. `isEnabled("digest_email", buildFlagContext(null, org))` gates the org. The flag is defined in `src/config/feature-flags.ts` with a plan strategy of `growth` or higher, and the org can override it via `enabledFlagOverrides`. Evaluation lives in `src/lib/feature-flags.ts`.

### 3. Who is subscribed

`listDigestRecipients()` in `src/server/services/digest-service.ts` calls `preferenceRepo.listDigestSubscribers()` in `src/server/repositories/notification-preference-repository.ts`. That returns the distinct `user_id`s in `notification_preferences` for this org where `digest_only = true`.

A member subscribes by setting `digestOnly` on at least one notification kind. This goes through `upsertPreference()`. The `email` and `inApp` flags are independent of this.

### 4. How one person's digest is built

**Upstream, the notification rows.** `src/server/services/notification-service.ts` subscribes to `issue.assigned`, `issue.overdue`, `comment.created` and `member.joined`. Each handler calls `notify()`, which calls `resolveChannels()` per recipient:
- No preference row means the defaults, `in_app` plus `email`.
- `digestOnly` keeps the in-app row and adds `email` only if the plan flag is on.
- If no channels remain, no row is written.

The `channels` column is recorded but never read for dispatch. `sendEmail` has only two callers, the digest job and `auth-service.ts` (welcome and password reset). So the digest is the only path that emails notifications.

**Downstream, per recipient in `runDigestEmailJob`:**
1. `buildDigest()` in `digest-service.ts` re-fetches the org and re-checks the flag. It then calls `notificationRepo.listUnreadSince()`, which returns rows where `read_at IS NULL` and `created_at >= now − 24h`, newest first. The window is rolling, not "since the last digest". The filter `createdAt <= windowEnd` is applied in JavaScript, and the result is sliced to `DIGEST_MAX_ENTRIES` (50). An empty result returns `null`.
2. `userRepo.findUserById()` loads the recipient. A missing user is skipped silently.
3. `renderDigest()` calls `renderEmail("digest", …)` in `src/server/services/email-service.ts`. That produces a generic key/value table containing `orgId`, `recipientName`, `entryCount`, `windowStart`, `windowEnd` and `headline` (the first entry's title). The subject is "Your Taskflow digest". The react-email `DigestEmail` in `src/emails/digest-email.tsx` and `renderTemplate()` in `src/emails/render.ts` are not on this path.
4. `sendEmail()` logs an `email.sent` line with the recipient, subject and body length.
5. Only after a successful send, `notificationRepo.markRead()` runs for each entry. This is the dedupe mechanism. A second run in the same window finds nothing unread.
6. `result.processed` is incremented. Errors are caught per recipient, `result.failed` is incremented and the error is logged. That recipient is not retried in the run.

### 5. Why a subscriber can get no email that day

Any one of these is enough:
- **No run in the org's hour.** The scheduler only starts in the Node runtime. A restart does not catch up on missed days. If nothing calls the cron route, nothing runs. Because the run minute comes from the process start time, a run that drifts outside the digest hour skips that day.
- **Org not among the 50 oldest-measured usage rows**, or it has no usage row at all.
- **Org archived.**
- **Plan below `growth`** and no `digest_email` override. This is checked in both the job and `buildDigest`.
- **Recipient user row missing.**
- **No unread notification in the last 24 hours.** This covers notifications already read in the app, notifications older than 24 hours after a missed run, and members whose channels were all off, so no row was written.
- **An exception while building or sending** for that recipient. It is logged and not retried.

### 6. Problems found while tracing

- **Org coverage is capped and unreliable.** The digest uses the usage rollup's list, limited to 50 and ordered by `measuredAt`. The rollup job uses 25. The digest job does not update `measuredAt`, so orgs beyond the first 50 are skipped on their hour, with no catch-up.
- **Overflow beyond 50 is dropped.** `buildDigest` keeps the 50 newest. The rest are never marked read and fall out of the next 24-hour window. The template's "…and N more" line cannot render because the bundle is already truncated.
- **`digestWindow()` is unused.** `src/lib/date.ts` has a digest-hour-aligned window function that is tested but not called. The job uses a rolling 24 hours, so the digest hour controls only when the job runs, not what it covers. The template's "since your last digest" wording doesn't match the behaviour.
- **The email is not the designed template.** Entry titles are not in the email at all. Only the count and the first title are sent. The subject omits the org name because `digest-service.ts` does not pass `orgName`.
- **Channel preferences are ignored.** `listUnreadSince` filters neither by kind nor by channel. A kind set to `email: false` can still appear in a digest.
- **Recipients are not checked for live membership.** Eligibility comes from preference rows alone. No code deletes those rows when a member is archived, and `findUserById` does not check whether the user is still in the org.
- **Possible double send.** `markRead` runs after the send and is not atomic. Overlapping runs from the scheduler and the cron route could send twice. Sequential runs are safe, as the test "does not resend" shows.
- **Dead and duplicated code.** The `digest.due` bridge is never triggered. The flag check runs in both the job and `buildDigest`.
